title: Oja's Rule Selects the Principal Statistical Direction While Bounding Weight Norm
alt: A flow diagram in which centered input produces a linear output, a Hebbian growth term combines with Oja normalization to update weights, and the result is a bounded principal covariance mode.
caption: For centered linear input, the Oja update combines the Hebbian term h x and weight-dependent decay \(-h^{2}w\) in one local rule. The first rotates w toward high-variance directions of the input covariance, while the second strengthens as output grows, allowing the direction to approach the principal eigenvector without unbounded norm growth. This conclusion assumes stationary input, a suitably small learning rate, and a nondegenerate largest eigenvalue.

questionDistractors.text: The decay term removes high-variance directions, making the weights align with the smallest covariance eigenvalue.
questionDistractors.explanation: Hebbian growth favors the largest-variance direction; decay controls magnitude rather than selecting the smallest component.

questionDistractors.text: Keeping only the Hebbian branch would yield the same bounded weights, because positive semidefinite covariance automatically stops their growth.
questionDistractors.explanation: Nonnegative covariance eigenvalues can sustain growth; removing stabilization does not guarantee bounded weights.

questionDistractors.text: The diagram guarantees convergence to the same principal component for every learning rate and for changing input statistics, without further conditions.
questionDistractors.explanation: Large steps and changing input statistics can violate the stated convergence conditions.

questionAnswer: Hebbian growth selects statistical directions; output-dependent decay controls the norm under suitable input and step-size conditions.

lectureTitle: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
title: The Negative Gradient Descends the Local Loss Slope
alt: A normalized one-dimensional convex loss curve with a sequence of gradient-descent iterates approaching its minimum.
caption: At the current parameter, the gradient points in the locally fastest direction of increasing loss, so update \(\Delta w=-\eta \nabla L\) moves in the opposite direction. The markers show only normalized iteration order, not experimental observations. They illustrate that an appropriate step can approach the minimum successively, whereas the Taylor approximation does not guarantee descent with an excessively large learning rate.

questionDistractors.text: Following the negative gradient guarantees that every step lowers loss and reaches the global minimum, regardless of the chosen learning rate.
questionDistractors.explanation: The direction is local; large steps can invalidate the first-order approximation and increase loss.

questionDistractors.text: Shrinking gaps between markers prove that the optimizer reduces its learning rate after every update.
questionDistractors.explanation: Smaller gradients also shrink steps at a fixed learning rate, so marker spacing alone cannot establish a schedule.

questionDistractors.text: The markers are biological measurements that determine real synaptic learning speed.
questionDistractors.explanation: These are normalized optimization illustrations, without empirical neural data or a biological time unit.

questionAnswer: The steps show negative-gradient descent with a suitable learning rate; oversized steps can still raise loss.

lectureTitle: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchies, Receptive Fields, and the LNP Model
title: From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field
alt: A flow diagram in which a retinal image patch passes through ON- and OFF-center-surround contrast channels and spatially arranged positive and negative subregions to produce an oriented Gabor-like linear drive.
caption: ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning.

questionDistractors.text: A circularly symmetric DoG already specifies a preferred orientation; subsequent spatial arrangement changes only gain and leaves selectivity unchanged.
questionDistractors.explanation: A circular kernel has no preferred orientation; elongated arrangements break rotational symmetry.

questionDistractors.text: Summing the total ON and OFF activity gives the same orientation tuning regardless of subfield positions, signs, or alignment along an axis.
questionDistractors.explanation: Orientation tuning depends on matching the signed spatial arrangement, so those details cannot be discarded.

questionDistractors.text: The feature maps copy absolute luminance rather than transforming the image.
questionDistractors.explanation: Feature maps represent filter matches and local contrast, not copies of pixel intensity.

questionAnswer: ON/OFF channels extract contrast; aligned signed subfields make matching orientations add coherently, producing orientation selectivity.

lectureTitle: Spike-Triggered Averaging and White-Noise System Identification
title: Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow
alt: A flow diagram showing white-noise stimulus histories passing through a linear projection and nonlinearity to generate spikes, after which pre-spike stimuli are aligned and averaged to produce an STA parallel to the filter direction.
caption: A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.

questionDistractors.text: Looking backward from spikes means future stimuli cause current responses, making STA an acausal encoding model.
questionDistractors.explanation: Reverse analysis describes an estimation procedure using earlier stimuli, not a reversal of physiological causality.

questionDistractors.text: The STA–filter relation holds for all stimulus distributions and even nonlinearities, and sufficient sampling always guarantees a nonzero STA that recovers the complete filter.
questionDistractors.explanation: Colored inputs can bias the STA, while even responses can cancel it even with abundant data.

questionDistractors.text: The STA alone determines the nonlinearity, noise distribution, and all future predictions.
questionDistractors.explanation: The STA primarily supplies directional information; nonlinearity, scale, and predictive validation require separate treatment.

questionAnswer: Forward LNP predicts spikes; reverse averaging estimates the filter direction when the white Gaussian single-feature STA is nonzero.

lectureTitle: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
title: A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor
alt: Three input branches represent stimulus history, a neuron's own spike history, and other neurons' histories; after filtering, they meet in a linear predictor whose inverse link produces a conditional spike probability.
caption: A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse.

questionDistractors.text: Each branch generates independent spikes that are summed, and the inverse link merely sets the plot's axis units.
questionDistractors.explanation: Branches combine into a linear predictor; the inverse link maps that predictor to a response mean or probability.

questionDistractors.text: Self-history and coupling branches may include current and future spikes, improving accuracy without leaking the response because the stimulus is also included in the model.
questionDistractors.explanation: Current targets and future events leak information; history covariates must precede the predicted event.

questionDistractors.text: Including stimulus input turns the coupling branch into a verified anatomical wiring map.
questionDistractors.explanation: Measured stimulus control cannot eliminate unobserved common drive or indirect interactions.

questionAnswer: Stimulus and histories combine in the predictor; the inverse link yields a conditional mean or probability, not an anatomical wiring map.

title: Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints
alt: A flow diagram in which a sensory signal with input noise passes through a linear encoder and output-noise channel to a decorrelated output code jointly constrained by retained information and output cost.
caption: Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality.

nodes.label:
Linear encoder A
signal + input noise

questionDistractors.text: Setting every encoder gain to zero is optimal because the channels become uncorrelated, which guarantees preservation of all sensory information.
questionDistractors.explanation: Zero gain also removes the signal; absent correlation is not a substitute for information retention.

questionDistractors.text: Output noise passes through the encoder with the signal, so a single fixed input covariance can replace all noise locations throughout optimization.
questionDistractors.explanation: Output noise is added after the encoder and cannot simply be treated as the same fixed input noise.

questionDistractors.text: Whitening uniquely determines each neuron's localized center–surround receptive field.
questionDistractors.explanation: Orthogonal rotations leave equivalent whitened codes; localized shapes need additional structural constraints.

questionAnswer: Signal and input noise pass through the encoder before output noise is added; information and output cost constrain redundancy reduction.

lectureTitle: Adaptation, Natural-Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
title: Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening
alt: A normalized spatial-frequency plot comparing ideal linearly rising whitening gain, a noise-aware band-pass response, and a narrower low-frequency response at lower signal-to-noise ratio.
caption: If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements.

questionDistractors.text: The high-frequency roll-off proves natural images contain no high-frequency structure and has nothing to do with optics or noise.
questionDistractors.explanation: High-frequency signals can exist yet be unreliable; roll-off reflects signal, noise, and optical limits.

questionDistractors.text: The curves are successive recordings over time from the same neuron.
questionDistractors.explanation: The horizontal axis is spatial frequency; the curves are normalized theoretical illustrations, not temporal measurements.

questionDistractors.text: The lower-SNR curve recommends unlimited amplification of the highest frequencies in dim light to reconstruct every edge perfectly without increasing any noise cost.
questionDistractors.explanation: Noise-dominated frequencies should not receive unlimited gain; lower SNR instead favors a narrower band and pooling.

questionAnswer: Ideal whitening increases gain with frequency; accounting for noise produces high-frequency roll-off, and lower SNR narrows the reliable band further.

lectureTitle: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrent Dynamics
title: After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection
alt: A normalized excitatory-inhibitory rate phase plane in which one E-nullcline intersects center and surround I-nullclines; the surround fixed point lies at lower excitatory and inhibitory rates.
caption: In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone.

questionDistractors.text: Shifting the I-nullcline upward must increase the final inhibitory rate, so the lower surround intersection can only be a plotting error.
questionDistractors.explanation: The joint intersection determines the final rates; movement of one curve is not itself a population-rate change.

questionDistractors.text: Every nullcline intersection necessarily attracts all nearby trajectories without further analysis.
questionDistractors.explanation: An intersection ensures zero derivatives; local dynamics still determine whether it is stable.

questionDistractors.text: The lower I rate proves that the additional surround drive is negative and that the excitatory subsystem no longer needs any inhibitory feedback to remain stable.
questionDistractors.explanation: In an ISN, positive I drive can lower steady-state I firing without removing inhibition's stabilizing role.

questionAnswer: The shifted I-nullcline can intersect at lower E and I rates; this identifies a steady state, whose stability still needs checking.

lectureTitle: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
title: In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes
alt: A flow diagram that transforms population activity from neuronal coordinates through V inverse into mode amplitudes, evolves them independently in diagonal eigenvalue space, and reconstructs neuronal activity with V.
caption: If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.

questionDistractors.text: Each mode is one anatomical neuron, so diagonalization proves that the original network contains no recurrent connections.
questionDistractors.explanation: Modes are population-coordinate directions, not individual cells; decoupling coordinates does not remove connections.

questionDistractors.text: Transforming activity while leaving input in neuron coordinates gives every mode the correct drive, because external inputs bypass the recurrent weight matrix and need no coordinate change.
questionDistractors.explanation: Inputs require the same inverse basis transform to determine the drive to each mode.

questionDistractors.text: Every positive eigenvalue produces growth regardless of intrinsic leak.
questionDistractors.explanation: The continuous-time equation includes leak; a positive real eigenvalue below one can still produce decay.

questionAnswer: For a diagonalizable matrix, the inverse basis transform separates activity into modes, transformed inputs drive them, and the original basis reconstructs neuronal activity.
